sections: What is inside a WiFi QR code?

The code holds a short text in a de-facto standard format that phones recognise: *WIFI:T:WPA;S:MyNetwork;P:MyPassword;H:false;;*. *T* is the security type, *S* the network name, *P* the password and *H* whether the network is hidden. Special characters such as ; , : and \ in the name or password are escaped automatically so the code works.

sections: **WPA2** has been the standard for home and office Wi-Fi since 2006 and is what most routers use. **WPA3**, introduced in 2018, adds stronger protection against password guessing; in the QR code it uses the same *WPA* type, so choose WPA/WPA2/WPA3. **WEP** is an obsolete, easily broken standard – if your router still uses it, upgrade the setting to WPA2 or WPA3. *No password* is only for open networks such as public hotspots with a login page.

For a table tent or wall sign, download the SVG and place it in Word, Canva or any design app at 4–6 cm wide. Add the network name and a short line such as *"Point your camera here to connect"* for people who have never scanned a Wi-Fi code. For Airbnb and holiday rentals, add it to the welcome book next to house rules; for hotels, print it on key-card holders. A frame with *Scan for Wi-Fi* built into the code makes the purpose obvious at a glance.

Make one code per network: for example a guest network on the ground floor and another for the meeting rooms. Name the downloads clearly and add the network name to each printed sign so staff can replace the right one when passwords change. Is it safe to share Wi-Fi with a QR code?

It is as safe as writing the password on a card: anyone who scans or photographs the code can read the password. That is fine for guest networks, but do not post a code for your main home or business network in public. The advantage of generating it here is that the password is never uploaded to a QR service while you create it.

Always print the network name and password in plain text near the code as well. Some visitors use phones without a camera app that reads QR codes, laptops cannot scan, and screen-reader users benefit from readable text. A code plus text is the friendliest setup for every guest, whatever device they carry.

sections: A QR (Quick Response) code was invented in 1994 by Denso Wave for tracking car parts and is now an ISO standard (ISO/IEC 18004). The black and white squares – *modules* – encode data in binary, with three large finder patterns in the corners that let a camera locate the code at any angle. Reed–Solomon error correction is built in, so a code still scans when it is partly dirty, scratched or covered by a logo. A single code holds up to about 7,000 digits or 2,953 bytes of text, but shorter content makes a simpler, easier-to-scan pattern.

Scanners look for dark modules on a light background. Keep a strong contrast – black, navy, dark green or dark brand colours on white or cream work well. Avoid light codes on dark backgrounds (inverted codes are not supported by every scanner), pale yellows and greys, and busy photo backgrounds. Gradients are fine when both ends stay dark.
Higher levels add more modules, so the code becomes denser; print it a little larger to compensate.
How big should you print a QR code?

A practical rule is a minimum of about 2 × 2 cm (0.8 in) for close-up scanning such as business cards and packaging, and roughly one tenth of the scanning distance for posters – a code read from 2 metres away should be about 20 cm wide. Always keep a quiet zone (empty margin) of at least four modules around the code, and use the SVG download for print so it stays razor-sharp at any size.
